claims.claim: Courthouses permit inspection of public court files while usable digital copies of those files are available only through private paid services.
Court records include complaints, motions, orders, and judgments that document exercises of state power.
In some jurisdictions, a court-record room open only during business hours can satisfy the applicable public-access rules.
Business-hours, in-person court-record access is practically inadequate for people working those hours, living far from the courthouse, or relying on screen readers.
Courts create court records through the exercise of public authority.
Private database companies gather public court-record material and improve its searchability.
Private court-record databases sell access to the resulting product at professional-market rates.
The search layer is the valuable component of private court-record database products.
The public supplies or funds the raw court-record material used by private databases.
People must pay separately for effective tools to find publicly produced court records.
Private court-record services clean court data, link dockets, and build powerful research tools.
Dependence on expensive private databases compounds inequality in access to court information.
Employers, landlords, reporters, researchers, and large firms can purchase broad visibility into court records.
Ordinary defendants may receive only narrow court-record access through confusing interfaces.
Paid or limited court-record access can leave formal legal rights unchanged while reducing a person's practical ability to exercise those rights.
Privacy redaction, security, system maintenance, and careful indexing of court records require meaningful work and resources.
